item.title: When Permutations and Combinations Work Together
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Permutations and combinations often appear in the same problem (if the two ideas are new, start with Understanding Permutations and Combinations with Examples). Whenever we must first select a group of items (a combination) and then arrange the chosen items in order (a permutation), we need both. This “choose first, arrange second” approach is the standard way to count when the items come from different categories.

NoteThe pattern

When there are several categories, Step 1 is a product of combinations, one per category, and is the size of the whole chosen group.

1. Passwords with a fixed mix of characters

Suppose we want a 4-character password made of 2 distinct letters (from 26) and 2 distinct digits (from 10). A single permutation formula cannot guarantee the exact mix, so we fix the mix first.

  • Step 1 (combination): choose the 2 letters and the 2 digits: groups.
  • Step 2 (permutation): arrange the 4 chosen characters: ways.
  • Total: passwords.

2. Code words from separate pools

We have 6 consonants and 4 vowels, and we want a 5-letter code word with exactly 3 consonants and 2 vowels (no letter repeated).

  • Step 1 (combination): ways to pick the letters.
  • Step 2 (permutation): arrange the 5 letters: orders.
  • Total: words.

3. A batting order

A cricket squad has 15 players: 8 batsmen and 7 bowlers. The coach picks a starting 11 with 6 batsmen and 5 bowlers, then sets the batting order.

  • Step 1 (combination): possible teams.
  • Step 2 (permutation): put the 11 players in order from #1 to #11: lineups.
  • Total: batting orders.

4. Seating guests on a stage

Twelve executives attend a conference, and 4 of them are chosen to sit in 4 labelled chairs on stage (Chair 1 to Chair 4).

  • Step 1 (combination): choose the 4 executives: groups.
  • Step 2 (permutation): assign the 4 chosen executives to the chairs: ways.
  • Total: ways.
TipA shortcut when there are no categories

Here nothing restricts who may sit where, so the two steps collapse into one:

Indeed, . The two-step method is needed when categories force a particular mix, as in the first three examples.

How to recognise these problems

The question asks for… Use
a group, order irrelevant combination only
an ordered arrangement of everything or of items from permutation only
a group with a required mix, and then an order combination(s) first, then

If the problem says “exactly of this kind and of that kind” and then asks for an arrangement, we are in the “choose first, arrange second” case.

item.title: Combinations When Some Items Are Always Selected or Always Omitted
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Choosing items from (see Understanding Permutations and Combinations with Examples for the basics) normally gives ways. But what if particular items must be included, or must not be? We start with a concrete team and let the logic show us the formula.

The situation

A coach must pick a team of players from a squad of . Without any condition there are teams. Now we add a condition, in two different versions.

Case 1: some items are always selected

The captain and the vice-captain () must both be on the team.

  1. The captain and vice-captain already hold 2 of the 5 spots, and their places are settled. They no longer take part in the choosing.
  2. The spots still open: .
  3. The players still available: (everyone except the captain and vice-captain).
  4. So the only real decision is which 3 of the other 8 join them:

Case 2: some items are always omitted

Instead, 2 players () are injured and must stay out.

  1. Injured players can never be picked, so we simply remove them from the squad: players remain.
  2. Nothing has been filled, so all 5 spots are still open.
  3. The decision is which 5 of the healthy 8 play:

Note

The two answers are equal here only by coincidence of the numbers: because choosing 3 players to include is the same as choosing 5 to leave out. The two cases are different problems in general.

item.title: Counting Rule and Addition Rule: When to Add and When to Multiply
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Counting problems usually come down to one question: do we add the numbers of ways, or multiply them? We answer it with two examples, then see why the common slogan is not quite right.

Multiplying: the counting rule

There are 3 ways to go from Sylhet to Dhaka, and 2 ways to go from Dhaka to Rajshahi. How many ways are there to get from Sylhet to Rajshahi?

We can list every route with a tree:

  • Sylhet to Dhaka by train, then Dhaka to Rajshahi by bus or train: 2 routes.
  • Sylhet to Dhaka by air, then bus or train: 2 routes.
  • Sylhet to Dhaka by bus, then bus or train: 2 routes.

The tree diagram above shows the same count.

Adding the same number three times is just multiplication, so we could have written

directly. This is the fundamental counting principle (the counting rule):

Note

If one stage can be done in ways and, whichever way it was done, a second stage can be done in ways, then the two stages together can be done in ways.

It is the building block behind permutations and combinations: see Understanding Permutations and Combinations with Examples for it in action.

Adding: the addition rule

To travel from Dhaka to Chattogram we can take one of 5 flights or one of 3 trains. We will take only one of them, so there is no second stage to carry out:

The addition rule applies when the options are alternatives that cannot happen together (and none is counted twice).

A better way to decide

The words “and” and “or” help only sometimes. A more reliable test is to ask whether the choice is finished after one pick.

Situation Is the choice complete? Operation
Sylhet to Rajshahi: we have reached Dhaka but not Rajshahi Incomplete: another stage is needed Multiply ()
Dhaka to Chattogram: one flight or one train Complete: the trip is done Add ()
  • Incomplete choices: keep multiplying until the whole task is complete.
  • Complete alternatives: add them.

Why “AND means multiply, OR means add” can mislead

In permutations, combinations and probability we often hear that AND leads to multiplication and OR leads to addition. That is a useful shortcut, but it has conditions.

  • Multiplication is valid when the number of ways (or the probability) at the second stage is the one that applies after the first stage. For counting, the second stage must have the same number of options whichever first option we took. For probabilities, we multiply by the conditional probability, which equals the plain probability only when the events are independent.
  • Addition is valid when the alternatives are mutually exclusive. If they can overlap, we must subtract the overlap.

In probability notation:

The first reduces to simple addition when (mutually exclusive events). The second reduces to when and are independent.

Using both in one problem

A bag has 6 red and 4 green balls. We draw 2 balls with replacement. What is the probability that both have the same colour?

Each way of getting “same colour” is a sequence of two draws, so each way is an incomplete choice until both draws are made (multiply). The two ways, red-red and green-green, are complete and cannot happen together (add):

TipWithout replacement

If the first ball is not put back, the second draw depends on the first, so we multiply by conditional probabilities instead:

We still multiply along each sequence and add the two exclusive outcomes.

Summary

  • Multiply stages that are carried out one after another until the task is complete.
  • Add complete, mutually exclusive alternatives.
  • Check the conditions (dependence and overlap) before applying the slogan.

item.title: Understanding Permutations and Combinations with Examples
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Two ideas sit behind most counting problems: arranging items and selecting them. We separate them on a tiny example first.

Permutation: order matters

How many ways can we arrange 2 letters taken from ?

That is 6 arrangements. A permutation is an arrangement, so and are different.

Combination: order does not matter

A combination is a selection, like choosing members for a team. Now we only ask which 2 letters are chosen:

That is 3 selections. Each one stands for two permutations: covers and , covers and , and covers and .

So

Both together: a 15-player squad

A team needs 11 players from a squad of 15, and then the 11 are placed in specific positions on the ground.

  1. Select the players: ways.
  2. Arrange the chosen 11: ways.
  3. By the counting rule, we multiply the two stages:

This is also the number of ways to arrange 11 players out of 15 directly, . It is the same relationship we saw with the letters:

This is an example of permutations and combinations used together, and also of the counting rule, which tells us when to multiply the number of ways. The counting rule itself, and when to add instead, is the subject of Counting Rule and Addition Rule: When to Add and When to Multiply.

The box method for permutations

There is a quick way to count permutations without a formula. Suppose we have 4 items, , and want to arrange 3 of them, with no item used twice.

Draw one box for each position:

  • The first box can take any of the 4 items.
  • Once one is used, 3 items are left for the second box.
  • Then 2 items are left for the third box.

We multiply because each box is an incomplete choice, exactly as the counting rule says (see Counting Rule and Addition Rule). The result is the same as .

When items can be repeated

If repetition is allowed, as with the digits of a number, nothing is used up. Every box has all 4 choices:

In general, boxes with choices each give arrangements.

Why it matters in real life: phone numbers

Mobile numbers in Bangladesh once had 9 digits: a 3-digit operator code (such as 019 or 017) followed by 6 digits. Each of the 6 positions can hold any of the 10 digits, so one code could supply

That was not enough for such a large population, so one more digit was added:

That was still not enough, so the numbers grew to 11 digits:

Many operators now hold two codes (for example 017 and 013), which doubles the supply to 20 crore numbers. Each extra digit multiplies the capacity by 10, which is why counting arguments like this matter for planning.

Where to go next

  • Many problems need both steps with several categories of items, such as a fixed mix of batsmen and bowlers: see When Permutations and Combinations Work Together.
  • If some items must always be in the selection, or must always be left out, the pool and spots shrink: see Combinations When Some Items Are Always Selected or Always Omitted.

item.title: When Complex Numbers Are More Natural Than So-Called Real Ones
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Complex numbers are the more natural choice whenever a problem involves rotations, oscillations, waves or roots of equations. Forcing a solution through real numbers alone needs messy trigonometry and heavy calculus, while complex numbers reduce the work to addition and multiplication. (If the basics are new, see Complex Numbers: Why They Are as Real as Real Numbers.)

Let’s go through six cases. In each we set the real-number approach beside the complex one.

1. Combining waves and oscillations

Real numbers: adding sound waves, light waves or alternating currents that start at different times (phases) needs trigonometric identities such as the one for .

Complex numbers: write each wave as a complex number. Its length is the wave’s strength (amplitude) and its angle is the timing (phase). Adding waves is then just adding numbers.

So the combined wave is , with no identities needed.

2. 2D rotations and geometry

Real numbers: rotating a point needs a matrix of sines and cosines.

Complex numbers: a point is one number, , and rotating it is one multiplication. This makes complex numbers a natural choice for 2D physics engines and robotics.

3. Differential equations

Real numbers: equations for vibrating springs, shock absorbers and RLC circuits often have solutions that oscillate while dying away. With real numbers we must guess combinations of sines, cosines and exponentials.

Complex numbers: growth, decay and oscillation are all one exponential, , with a complex . We just solve a quadratic.

The real part gives the decay () and the imaginary part gives the oscillation, so the solutions are and . No guessing was needed.

4. Roots of polynomials

Real numbers: has no solution, while has two. The degree alone does not tell us how many roots to expect.

Complex numbers: they are algebraically closed: every polynomial of degree has exactly roots (counting repeats). This makes stability analysis in control theory predictable.

5. 2D fluid flow and electromagnetism

Real numbers: describing air flow around a wing, or an electric field around a wire, needs coupled partial differential equations in and .

Complex numbers: complex functions preserve angles (conformal mapping). For ideal, frictionless flow, we can solve the easy case of flow around a circle, then use one complex function to bend the circle into another shape. The classic map turns a slightly off-centre circle into a wing-like profile, and the flow around the circle is carried along with it.

6. Hard real integrals

Real numbers: many integrals, especially in physics and statistics, have no elementary antiderivative, so ordinary calculus gets stuck.

Complex numbers: step into the complex plane and use the residue theorem. The answer is still a real number.

Summary

Problem Real-number approach Complex approach
Adding waves Trig identities Add two numbers
2D rotation matrix Multiply by
Oscillating, decaying solutions Guess sines, cosines, exponentials Solve a quadratic, read off
Counting roots Depends on the equation Always exactly
Flow around shapes Coupled PDEs Map a simple shape with one function
Hard integrals No elementary antiderivative Residues

Key takeaway

  • Whenever the problem involves a cycle, a rotation or a wave, complex numbers describe it directly.
  • They do not replace real numbers: the final answers (amplitudes, positions, integrals) are still real. Complex numbers are the shortcut we take to reach them.

item.title: Complex Numbers in Statistics: Where They Quietly Do the Work
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
Complex numbers act as a mathematical shortcut in statistics: they turn messy calculus and probability problems into simple algebra. If complex numbers are new to us, the earlier post on complex numbers covers the basics. Here we only need one fact: is a point on the unit circle.

1. Characteristic functions

Every probability distribution has a “fingerprint” called its characteristic function:

Unlike the moment-generating function, it exists for every distribution, because always stays on a circle of radius 1 and never explodes. That includes chaotic ones such as the Cauchy distribution, where the mean and variance do not exist.

Example: adding independent variables

For a coin flip (1 with probability , otherwise 0):

The total of two independent flips would normally need a convolution (a sum or integral over all ways to get each total). With characteristic functions, adding independent variables just multiplies them:

This is exactly the characteristic function of a Binomial(2, ), which is the right answer. Calculus has become multiplication.

Example: why the Cauchy average never settles

The standard Cauchy distribution has . For the average of independent Cauchy values, we multiply copies and rescale by :

The average has the same distribution as a single observation. Collecting more data never helps, which is why the law of large numbers fails for the Cauchy. The same machinery is the standard proof route for the central limit theorem: the characteristic function of a standardised average approaches , that of the normal distribution.

2. Circular statistics: averaging angles

Real numbers struggle with angles. The directions and are only 20 degrees apart, yet their ordinary average is

which points the opposite way. On the complex unit circle, each angle becomes the point . We average the points, then read off the angle:

The sines cancel (), leaving a point on the positive real axis. Its angle is , the sensible answer. The length of the average, 0.985, is also useful: it is close to 1 when the angles are tightly clustered and close to 0 when they are spread all around.

This is how statisticians average wind directions, bird migration paths, times of day and circadian rhythms.

3. Time series and spectral analysis

When data fluctuates over time (ocean tides, brain waves, monthly sales), the Fourier transform maps it into complex numbers whose sizes show which cycles are present. A series with a yearly rhythm in monthly data shows a peak at a period of 12 months. Spectral analysis is a standard way to find hidden cycles and periodic trends.

4. Complex normal data

In radar, wireless communication and MRI, each measurement arrives as an amplitude and a phase, that is, a pair of numbers. Writing the pair as one complex number keeps the geometry intact (size and angle) instead of splitting it into two separate real values, and gives a compact way to model signal plus noise.

Why this is useful

Idea Without complex numbers With complex numbers
Sum of independent variables Convolution (an integral) Multiply characteristic functions
Existence of a transform Moment-generating function may not exist Characteristic function always exists
Averaging angles and give Gives , as it should
Two-part measurements Two separate real values One complex value

Key takeaway

  • Complex numbers are not a curiosity in statistics: they make sums of random variables, proofs and angle averages simpler.
  • The unit-circle point is the key object, since it stays bounded and encodes angles naturally.

item.title: Waves and Turns: Why Complex Numbers Beat Trigonometry
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Mahmud
item.description:
A boatman who keeps changing direction, and waves that start at different times, are the same kind of problem, and both are clumsy with trigonometry. (In an earlier post we saw that complex numbers handle them easily.) Let’s work through examples both ways, starting with the boatman.

The idea

A boat leg, a distance in a heading , is the arrow : length , angle . A wave with strength and timing works the same way, as the arrow . In both cases:

  • Adding waves (or legs) is adding arrows.
  • Turning by an angle is multiplying by .

Example 1: a boatman who turns

A boatman rows 4 km east, turns left by 60°, and rows 3 km. How far is he from the start, and in which direction?

The trigonometry way

The two legs and the straight line back to the start form a triangle. The angle inside the triangle at the turn is (an easy place to slip).

  1. Law of cosines for the distance:

  2. Law of sines for the direction at the start:

    (The sine rule can give two possible angles, so we must check that the acute one is right.)

The complex way

East is the direction . After a 60° left turn he faces :

Distance: km. Direction: north of east. The same result with no triangle drawing and no ambiguity.

Example 2: he turns again

After the second leg, the boatman turns left by another 45° and rows 2 km more. His heading is now .

The trigonometry way

We must start a new triangle with the result so far (6.08 km at 25.3°) and the new leg (2 km at 105°):

  1. Angle between them: , so the angle inside the triangle is .
  2. Law of cosines: , so km.
  3. Law of sines: , so .
  4. Direction: .

Every extra leg needs a new triangle, a new interior angle to track, and the earlier rounding errors carry along.

The complex way

The third leg is just another arrow, . Add it to what we have:

Distance: km. Direction: . A fourth leg would be one more term.

Example 3: two waves

The trigonometry way
